'''''Ficus sycomorus''''', called the '''sycamore fig''' or the '''fig-mulberry''' (because the leaves resemble those of the [[mulberry]]), '''sycamore''', or '''sycomore''', is a [[ficus|fig]] species that has been cultivated since ancient times.<ref name="Zohary"/>

== Description ==

''Ficus sycomorus'' grows to {{Convert|20|m}} tall and has a considerable spread, with a dense round crown of spreading branches. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is green-yellow to orange and exfoliates in papery strips to reveal the yellow inner bark.  Like all other figs, it contains a [[latex]]. The [[leaves]] are heart-shaped with a round apex, {{Convert|14|cm|frac=4}} long by 10 cm wide, and arranged spirally around the twig. They are dark green above and lighter with prominent yellow veins below, and both surfaces are rough to the touch. The petiole is {{Convert|0.5–3|cm|abbr=on|frac=8}} long and pubescent.

Flowering and fruiting occurs year-round, starting in April or later depending on variety, peaking from July to December. The [[fruit]] is a large edible fig, 2–3 cm in diameter, ripening from buff-green to yellow or red. It is borne in thick clusters on long branchlets or the leaf axil. It is sometimes separated into five successive "crops".<ref name=":0" />

=== Etymology ===
The specific name came into English in the 14th century as ''sicamour'', derived from Old French ''sagremore, sicamor''. This in turn derives from Latin {{lang|la|sycomorus}}, from [[Ancient Greek]] {{lang|grc|σῡκόμορος}} ({{translit|grc|sykómoros}}) 'fig-mulberry'. The Greek name may be from the Greek tree-names {{translit|grc|sykón}} '[[fig]]' and {{translit|grc|moron}} '[[mulberry]]', or it may derive from the Hebrew name for the mulberry, {{translit|he|shiqmah}}.<ref>{{cite web |title=Sycamore (n.) |url=https://www.etymonline.com/word/sycamore |website=Online Etymology Dictionary |access-date=30 November 2024}}</ref>

The name ''[[sycamore]]'' spelled with an A has also been used for unrelated trees: the great maple, ''[[Acer pseudoplatanus]]'', or plane trees, ''[[Platanus]]''. The spelling  "sycomore", with an O rather than an A as the second vowel is, if used, specific to ''F. sycomorus''.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/sycomore | title=sycomore | work=Merriam-Webster.com | access-date=2016-10-30}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.collinsdictionary.com/dictionary/english/sycamore | access-date=2016-10-30 | title=sycamore | work=Collins English Dictionary }}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==

''Ficus sycomorus'' is native to [[Africa]] south of the [[Sahel]] and north of the [[Tropic of Capricorn]], excluding the central-west [[rainforest]] areas. It grows naturally in [[Lebanon]]; in the southern [[Arabian Peninsula]]; in [[Cyprus]]; in very localised areas in [[Madagascar]]; and in [[Palestinian territories|Palestine]] and [[Egypt]]. It also grows in Israel.<ref>{{Cite web |title=KKL-JNF: Trees in the Land of the Bible |url=https://www.kkl-jnf.org/files/people_and_environment/Israeli_Jewish_Festivals_and_Special_Days/tu_bishvat/Trees_of_Israel_English.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The Jerusalem Botanical Gardens Garden Explorer |url=https://jbg.gardenexplorer.org/taxon-28236.aspx}}</ref> In its native habitat, the tree is usually found in rich soils along rivers and in mixed woodlands.<ref>{{Cite web |title=SANBI Ficus sycomorus L. subsp. sycomorus |url=https://pza.sanbi.org/ficus-sycomorus-subsp-sycomorus%C2%A0}}</ref>

F. sycomorus is currently threatened by environmental destruction, but in spite of this, has demonstrated resilience. Considering the tree's healing qualities and traditional significance, scientific study and conservation efforts are imperative.<ref>{{Cite journal |last2=Ngugi |first2=Mathew |last3=Gitahi |first3=Stephen |last4=Machocho |first4=Alex |last1=Eunice Wothaya Muthee1, Mathew Ngugi1, Stephen Gitahi2, Alex Machocho1 |title=Scientific Research and Technology: Ficus Sycomorus: Ecological, Cultural, And Medicinal Insights into A Timeless Tree. |journal=International Journal of Scientific Research and Technology |date=2025 |volume=02 |issue=4 |pages=342–347 |doi=10.5281/zenodo.15236250 |url=https://www.ijsrtjournal.com/article/Ficus-Sycomorus:-Ecological,-Cultural,-And-Medicinal-Insights-into-A-Timeless-Tree}}</ref> 

==Cultivation==

Two major varieties are known in Egypt: Roumi (also called Falaki or Turki), which has more horizontally spread branches, stouter shoots and petioles, more densely spaced leaves that are wider than they are long, and larger, flatter, broad pink fruits; and Kelabi (also called Arabi or Beledi), which has more vertical branches, is more slender, has smaller leaves and has smaller yellowish pear shaped fruits.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Brown |first1=Thomas W. |last2=Walsingham |first2=F. G. |title=The Sycamore Fig In Egypt|journal=Journal of Heredity |url=https://academic.oup.com/jhered/article-abstract/8/1/3/835258?redirectedFrom=PDF |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=3–12 |doi=10.1093/jhered/8.1.3 |year=1917 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> In modern history, many Egyptians would once a year (on the day of a particular saint) make a ring of bruises and cuts around the base of their sycamore trees.{{why|date=March 2024}}<ref name=":0"/>

[[File:Ancient figs (Egypt 2000-1500 BC).jpg|thumb|left|Some ancient ''Ficus sycomorus'' figs. [[Ancient Egyptian funerary practices|Egyptian tomb offering]], 2000-1500 BCE. At the [[Louvre]].]]

According to [[botany|botanists]] [[Daniel Zohary]] and Maria Hopf, cultivation of this species was "almost exclusively" by the [[ancient Egypt]]ians.<ref name="Zohary" /> Remains of ''F. sycomorus'' begin to appear in predynastic times and occur in quantity from the start of the [[third millennium BC]]. It was the ancient Egyptian [[tree of life]].<ref>{{cite book |title=Death and salvation in ancient Egypt |first1=Jan |last1=Assmann |first2=David |last2=Lorton |others=translated by David Lorton |page=171 |publisher=Cornell University Press |year=2005 |isbn=978-0-8014-4241-4}}</ref> Zohary and Hopf note that "the fruit and the timber, and sometimes even the twigs, are richly represented in the [[tomb]]s of the Egyptian Early, Middle and Late Kingdoms."<ref name="Zohary"/> In numerous cases the parched fruiting bodies, known as [[Syconium|sycons]], "bear characteristic gashing marks indicating that this art, which induces ripening, was practised in Egypt in ancient times."<ref name="Zohary">{{cite book |first1=Daniel |last1=Zohary |first2=Maria |last2=Hopf |title=Domestication of plants in the Old World |edition=fourth |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2012 |pages=130–131}}</ref>

Although this species of fig requires the presence of the [[symbiotic]] [[wasp]] ''[[Ceratosolen]] arabicus'' to reproduce sexually, and this insect is extinct in Egypt, Zohay and Hopf have no doubt that Egypt was "the principal area of sycamore fig development."<ref name="Zohary"/> Some of the caskets of mummies in [[Egypt]] are made from the wood of this tree. In tropical areas where the wasp is common, complex mini-ecosystems involving the wasp, nematodes,<ref name="Susoy 2016">{{cite journal |last1=Susoy |first1=Vladislav |last2=Herrmann |first2=Matthias |last3=Kanzaki |first3=Natsumi |last4=Kruger |first4=Meike |last5=Nguyen |first5=Chau N. |last6=Rödelsperger |first6=Christian |last7=Röseler |first7=Waltraud |last8=Weiler |first8=Christian |last9=Giblin-Davis |first9=Robin M. |last10=Ragsdale |first10=Erik J. |last11=Sommer |first11=Ralf J. |title=Large-scale diversification without genetic isolation in nematode symbionts of figs |journal=Science Advances |year=2016 |volume=2 |issue=1 |article-number=e1501031 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.1501031 |pmid=26824073 |pmc=4730855 |bibcode=2016SciA....2E1031S }}</ref><ref name="Kruger 2021">{{cite journal |last1=Kruger |first1=Meike S. |last2=Kanzaki |first2=Natsumi |last3=Giblin-Davis |first3=Robin M. |last4=Greeff |first4=Jaco M. |title=Molecular diversity and relationships of fig associated nematodes from South Africa |journal=PLOS ONE |date=10 August 2021 |volume=16 |issue=8 |article-number=e0255451 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0255451 |pmid=34375357 |pmc=8354458 |bibcode=2021PLoSO..1655451K |doi-access=free }}</ref> other parasitic wasps, and various larger predators revolve around the life cycle of the fig. The trees' random production of fruit in such environments assures its constant attendance by the insects and animals which form this ecosystem.

Sycomores were often planted around artificial pools in ancient Egyptian gardens.<ref name=":2">{{citation |chapter=The Sycamore in Ancient Egypt |first1=Mohammed F. |last1=Azzazy |first2=Azza |last2=Ezzat |title= Liber Amicorum–Speculum Siderum: Nūt Astrophoros Archaeopress Egyptology |date=2016 |publisher= Archaeopress |isbn= 978-1-78491-523-0}}.</ref>

The sycamore tree was brought to the Southern Levant, also known as Israel, by [[Philistines]] during the Iron Age, along with [[opium poppy]] and [[cumin]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2015/08/150828112741.htm |title=Philistines introduced sycamore, cumin and opium poppy into Israel during the Iron Age |newspaper=Science daily |date=28 August 2015 |access-date=25 October 2015}}.</ref><ref>{{Citation |title=Nature |journal=Scientific Reports |date=25 August 2015 |volume=5 |issue=1 |article-number=13308 |doi=10.1038/srep13308 |last1=Frumin |first1=Suembikya |last2=Maeir |first2=Aren M. |last3=Kolska Horwitz |first3=Liora |last4=Weiss |first4=Ehud |pmid=26304818 |pmc=4642518}}.</ref>  Prior to the Iron Age, the existence of the sycamore is not found in Canaanite, Israelite, Judahite, and Phoenician sites.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Philistines introduced sycamore, cumin and opium poppy into Israel during the Iron Age |url=https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/885502}}</ref> These sycamore trees used to be numerous in western [[Beirut]], lending their name to the neighborhood of Gemmayzeh (({{lang|ar|الْجُمَّيْزَة}} {{transliteration|ar|DIN|al-Ǧummayzah}}), "sycamore fig"). However, the trees have largely disappeared from this area.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.dailystar.com.lb/News/Lebanon-News/2005/Aug-31/6628-gemmayzeh-changing-new-habits-come-to-an-old-quarter.ashx |newspaper=[[The Daily Star (Lebanon)|The Daily Star]] |access-date=16 November 2021 |date= 31 August 2005 |title=Gemmayzeh changing: new habits come to an old quarter |first1=Jim |last1=Quilty |first2=Leila |last2=Diab |quote=... named after a sycamore tree that was once a landmark here.}}</ref>

== Therapeutic Uses ==
The tree has great medicinal value, since the fruit, bark, leaves, and even the latex are anti-inflammatory in nature. As a result, it has traditionally been used for digestive problems, and shows future potential for the development of therapy for chronic inflammatory illness. In addition, it is useful for the treatment of respiratory issues, and diabetes, as well as wound care.<ref>{{Cite web |last2=Ngugi |first2=Mathew |last3=Gitahi |first3=Stephen |last4=Machocho |first4=Alex |last1=Eunice Wothaya Muthee1, Mathew Ngugi1, Stephen Gitahi2, Alex Machocho1 |title=International Journal of Scientific Research and Technology |date=2025 |volume=03 |issue=4 |pages=342–347 |doi=10.5281/zenodo.15236250 |url=https://www.ijsrtjournal.com/article/Ficus-Sycomorus-Ecological-Cultural-And-Medicinal-Insights-into-A-Timeless-Tree}}</ref>

== Practical Uses ==
In Africa, the wood of the tree is used as fuel, both firewood and for charcoal.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ficus sycomorus |url=https://apps.worldagroforestry.org/treedb/AFTPDFS/Ficus_sycomorus.PDF}}</ref>

===Gardens===
In the [[Near East]] ''F. sycomorus'' is an orchard and [[ornamental tree]] of great importance and extensive use. It has wide-spreading branches and [[shade tree|affords shade]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ficus sycomorus |url=https://worldplants.ca/display0.php?id=10073}}</ref>

== In culture ==

=== Judaism and Christianity ===
[[File:CairoVirginTree.jpg|alt=CairoVirginTree|thumb|The "Tree of the Virgin" in Egypt.]]
In the [[Hebrew Bible]], the sycomore is mentioned seven times ({{langx|hbo|שִׁקְמָה|shiqmā}}; Strong's number 8256.) This quote from Kings demonstrates that it was common in Biblical times: "And the king (Solomon) made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar as common as the sycamore trees that are in the lowland, because of their abundance.” (I Kings 10:27.)<ref>{{Cite web |title=KKL-JNF: Trees in the Land of the Bible |url=https://www.kkl-jnf.org/files/people_and_environment/Israeli_Jewish_Festivals_and_Special_Days/tu_bishvat/Trees_of_Israel_English.pdf}}</ref> It is also mentioned once in the [[New Testament]] ({{langx|grc-x-koine|συκομoραία|sykomoraia}} or {{lang|grc|συκομορέα}} {{transliteration|grc|ALA-LC|sykomorea}};<ref>{{LSJ|sukomore/a|συκομορέα|ref}}.</ref> Strong's number 4809). It was a popular and valuable fruit tree in [[Jericho]] and [[Canaan]].<ref name="moldenke 106 108">{{cite book |last=Moldenke |first=Harold N. |title=Plants of the Bible |date=1952 |publisher= Chronica Botanica Company |location=Waltham, Massachusetts USA |pages=106–108}}</ref>

In [[El Matareya, Cairo|El Matareya]], there is a sycamore known as the Tree of the Virgin, which serves as a pilgrimage site. It is not the same tree; instead, when the previous tree that stands in this spot dies, a new one is planted from cuttings of the old tree.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-18 |title=The Virgin's Tree in Egypt: A Story of Survival |url=https://www.photorientalist.org/exhibitions/egypts-virgin-tree-story-survival/article/ |access-date=2024-02-24 |website=Photorientalist |language=en-US}}</ref> It is said that the Holy Family took refuge in this tree.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Sachs |first=Susan |date=2001-12-26 |title=Cairo Journal; A Tree Drooping With Its Ancient Burden of Faith |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/12/26/world/cairo-journal-a-tree-drooping-with-its-ancient-burden-of-faith.html |access-date=2024-02-24 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> The [[Pope of the Coptic Orthodox Church|Coptic pope]] Theophilus also recounted that [[Joseph (Bible)|Joseph]] had a walking stick, which an infant [[Jesus]] broke. When Joseph buried the pieces of the stick, a sycamore grew forth and provided shelter.<ref>{{Cite web |last=El-Aref |first=Nevine |title=Virgin Mary Site Inaugurated |url=https://english.ahram.org.eg/NewsContent/50/1207/476492/AlAhram-Weekly/Heritage/Virgin-Mary-site-inaugurated.aspx}}</ref>

=== Other religions ===

In Ancient Egypt, the sycamore was associated with the goddesses [[Hathor]], [[Isis]], and [[Nut (goddess)|Nut]]. In the case of the latter, prayers exist referring to the "sycamore of Nut", and asking for water and breath. These goddesses were sometimes depicted as trees, sometimes standing in front of them with vessels of water, or sometimes as a tree with human body parts, such as an arm or breast. It was the most significant depicted life giving tree in ancient Egypt.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=R. Osborne |first=William |title=The Tree of Life in Ancient Egypt and the Book of Proverbs |journal=Journal of Ancient Near Eastern Religions}}</ref> Sycamores are referenced in ancient Egyptian love poetry as a meeting place for lovers.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2"/> There are references to twin sycamores of [[turquoise]] in funerary contexts which [[Ra]] comes forth from, indicating they likely face east,<ref name=":1"/> or are located on the eastern horizon.<ref name=":2"/>

In modern Egyptian folklore, the sycamore retains an association with mysticism and magic. In the story "It Serves Me Right!", it is used to represent the Tree of Lifespans. The fruit from this tree dries up at the end of a life, but is fresh when one still has more life to live. Therefore, the inhabitants of a land found at the bottom of a well in the story only eat the dry, bad sycamore fruits and leave the good ones alone.<ref>{{Cite book |last=El-Shamy |first=Hasan |title=Folktales of Egypt |date=1980 |publisher=The University of Chicago Press |isbn=0-226-20624-6 |pages=87–93}}</ref>

In [[Kikuyu people|Kikuyu religion]], the sycomore is a sacred tree. All sacrifices to [[Ngai]] (or Murungu), the supreme creator, were performed under the tree. The name of the Kikuyu tribe is derived from the name of the tree in Kikuyu (''Mũkũyũ''). Some of those ceremonies carried out under the tree are still observed.<ref>{{Cite web |url= https://mukuyu.wordpress.com/2008/11/13/origins/ |title= Gikuyu Origins |date= 13 November 2008 |access-date= 9 April 2015 |website= Mukuyu }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title= African Religions and Philosophy |last= Mbiti |first= John |publisher= Oxford University Press |year= 1990 }}</ref>
